Part B · Chapter B6

Making deep networks trainable

Starting weights, normalisation and shortcuts for deep networks, and dropout to reduce overfitting

In a network with twenty layers, the signal (the numbers passed forward) and the slopes from backpropagation can shrink or grow layer after layer, so training can fail. This chapter shows the problem, then three remedies (the scale of the starting weights, normalisation, residual connections) and dropout, which adds noise to reduce overfitting. The figures use random networks with made-up weights and made-up hidden values for six sharks.

You will need: backpropagation and the vanishing slope (B4), the variance and standardising (0.7), a neuron with an activation (B1) and feature scaling (A2).

Signals through twenty layers

Guess first. A network has 20 layers of 100 tanh units. Its weights start as random numbers with standard deviation 0.01 (the weight spread \(\sigma\)), and its inputs have typical size 1 (the square root of their average square). About how large are the activations, the outputs of the units, in layer 20: about 1, about 0.001, or smaller than \(10^{-15}\)?

At the start of training, a layer multiplies the typical size of its inputs by its size factor, which depends on \(\sigma\). A size factor of 0.1, applied 20 times, leaves \(10^{-20}\) of the starting size, and a size factor of 2 gives about \(10^{6}\) times it. For ReLU units (which output their input if positive and 0 otherwise), only a size factor close to 1 keeps the size near its start. A tanh unit never outputs more than 1, so with large weights its activations stay near 1 and its slopes grow instead. Backpropagation sends the slopes (gradients) back through the same weights, so they can shrink or grow too.

  1. The weights are random and made up. Choose “too small: spread 0.01”: in the line plot the activations fall in a straight line, a constant factor per layer, to \(1.1\times10^{-20}\) at layer 20.
  2. Switch to ReLU and choose “too large: spread 1”: the activations reach \(1.7\times10^{17}\) at layer 20.

At spread 0.01 the activations fall to about \(10^{-20}\) by layer 20, below \(10^{-15}\); at spread 0.141 activations and slopes stay near their start.

How it works

Take the guess. A tanh unit adds up its 100 inputs multiplied by random weights to get its total input \(z\). It outputs \(\tanh(z)\), a number between \(-1\) and 1 that is close to \(z\) when \(z\) is small. For inputs of typical size 1 and \(\sigma = 0.01\), \(z\) has typical size 0.1, as the equation below shows. So the activations of layer 1 have size about 0.1. The later layers multiply it by 0.1 again, so layer 20 has size \(0.1^{20} = 10^{-20}\).

\(\mathrm{Var}(z)\)variance of \(z\): 0.01=\(n\)inputs: 100×\(\sigma^2\)variance of a weight: 0.0001×\(\mathbb{E}[x^2]\)average square of an input: 1→\(\sqrt{0.01} = 0.1\)typical size of \(z\)

The equation applies to random weights with mean 0, independent of one another and of the inputs. The variance of \(z\) is then the sum of \(\sigma^2 x_i^2\) over the \(n\) inputs \(x_i\). So a layer multiplies the average square by the square factor \(n\sigma^2\) and the typical size by the size factor \(\sqrt{n\sigma^2}\), while tanh stays close to linear.

Common belief. Starting at zero is neutral, and small random weights are safe.

Why it fails. A spread of 0.01 still multiplies the size by 0.1 per layer. A start at 0 fails differently. With all weights and biases 0, the slopes of the weights are 0, so no weight changes. Units with equal incoming and outgoing weights also stay identical, so a layer of 100 such units acts as one unit.

Better account. Start at random, with \(\sigma\) chosen so that \(n\sigma^2\) is close to 1 (next section).

Quick quiz

With \(n = 100\) and \(\sigma = 0.1\), what is the square factor of a tanh layer, and what does that predict for layer 20?

\(n\sigma^2 = 100 \times 0.01 = 1\), so the average square and the size should stay near their start. In the figure (the “Xavier: spread 0.1” entry) the size is 0.16 at layer 20, below its start. It falls because a tanh output is smaller in size than its input, and the difference grows with the size of the input.

Why must the size factor of one layer be close to 1, when only the product over 20 layers matters?

The size at layer 20 is the starting size times the product of 20 size factors. If the size factor is 0.5 in all layers, the product is about \(10^{-6}\), and if it is 0.9, the product is 0.12. A small difference in a layer grows with depth.

Terms

initialisation
choosing the starting values of the weights, usually at random
weight spread \(\sigma\)
the standard deviation of the random starting weights (0.7)
vanishing and exploding
a signal or slope that shrinks or grows layer after layer (B4)
square factor, or variance factor
the factor \(n\sigma^2\) by which a layer multiplies the average square of the signal; its square root, the size factor, multiplies the typical size
symmetry
units in a layer that start with the same incoming and outgoing weights, and so stay identical

Reading the figure

Pick the initialisations in turn, then switch between tanh and ReLU. With zeros the activation table is one stripe at 0, and so is the slope table, except that with tanh the last layer keeps a slope. With too small the activations collapse toward 0 layer after layer. With too large a tanh network saturates (units pile up at \(\pm1\), where the slope is near 0), and a ReLU network explodes. Xavier is meant for tanh and shrinks a ReLU network, and He is meant for ReLU. The slope tables (right) are the backward pass of B4 on random numbers. They show how big the slope reaching a layer is, from a slope of size 1 at layer 20. A row of a table is one layer, and darker cells contain more units. The line plot gives the typical size on a log axis, so a straight line down is a constant factor per layer.

Where the factor comes from

The size of the signal follows a short calculation. A unit adds up \(n\) inputs times weights: \(z = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i\). If the weights have mean 0 and spread \(\sigma\), and are independent of the inputs, the terms \(w_i x_i\) are uncorrelated, so their variances add: \(\mathrm{Var}(z) = \sum_i \mathrm{Var}(w_i x_i) = n\,\sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}[x^2]\). For one term, the mean of \(w_i x_i\) is 0 because the mean of \(w_i\) is 0. Its variance is then \(\mathbb{E}[w_i^2 x_i^2] = \mathbb{E}[w_i^2]\,\mathbb{E}[x_i^2] = \sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}[x_i^2]\), since \(w_i\) and \(x_i\) are independent. One layer multiplies the average square by \(n\sigma^2\) (before the activation). That is a constant factor per layer as long as no tanh unit is saturated, which is why the lines in the plot are straight in those cases.

\[ z = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i \qquad \mathrm{Var}(z) = n\,\sigma^{2}\,\mathbb{E}[x^{2}] \]

  • \(n\) is the number of inputs of a unit, \(w_i\) a random weight with spread \(\sigma\) and \(x_i\) an input. \(\mathbb{E}[x^{2}]\) is the average square of an input.
  • The factor \(n\sigma^{2}\) multiplies the average square of the signal in a layer, and the next layer starts from the result.

The ReLU case with numbers

nσ² ÷ 2100 × 0.01² ÷ 2, ReLU=0.005variance factor per layer→ 20 layers →(0.005)20 ≈ 10−46variance, so size about 10−23|nσ² ÷ 2100 × 1 ÷ 2, spread 1=50per layer→5020 ≈ 1034variance, size about 1017

The box is a worked example for ReLU units (the factor \(n\sigma^2/2\) is explained in the next section). With spread 0.01, a layer cuts the variance to 0.5% of its size, so 20 layers leave a size of about \(10^{-23}\). With spread 1 a layer multiplies the variance by 50, and the size after 20 layers is about \(10^{17}\). The same factor, raised to the 20th power, explains both ends. The tanh case with spread 0.01 is the guess-first question: \(n\sigma^2 = 0.01\) per layer, so the size falls by a factor of \(0.1\) per layer, and \(0.1^{20}\) gives \(10^{-20}\), which matches the \(1.1\times10^{-20}\) of the figure.

A tanh example with numbers

Take spread 0.05 and width 100. The factor is \(n\sigma^2 = 100\times0.0025 = 0.25\) in variance, so the size falls by \(\sqrt{0.25} = 0.5\) per layer, and \(0.5^{20} \approx 10^{-6}\). The code runs the forward pass of a random tanh network for six spreads and sends a slope of size 1 back from layer 20. It uses its own random numbers, so the digits differ a little from the figure.

import numpy as np

n, depth, batch = 100, 20, 256
rms = lambda a: np.sqrt((a ** 2).mean())

def tanh_net(sigma, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Ws = [rng.standard_normal((n, n)) * sigma for _ in range(depth)]
    x = rng.standard_normal((batch, n))                  # inputs of typical size 1
    hs = []
    for W in Ws:
        x = np.tanh(x @ W); hs.append(x)
    g = rng.standard_normal((batch, n))                  # a slope of typical size 1 at layer 20
    for W, h in zip(reversed(Ws), reversed(hs)):
        g = (g * (1 - h ** 2)) @ W.T                     # one layer back (the B4 rule)
    return rms(hs[0]), rms(hs[9]), rms(hs[-1]), rms(g)

print("spread   layer 1   layer 10   layer 20   slope at layer 1")
for sigma in (0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.141, 0.3, 1.0):
    a1, a10, a20, g1 = tanh_net(sigma)
    print(f"{sigma:6.3f}   {a1:7.1e}   {a10:8.1e}   {a20:8.1e}   {g1:8.1e}")
spread   layer 1   layer 10   layer 20   slope at layer 1
 0.010   9.9e-02    9.1e-11    9.0e-21    9.3e-21
 0.050   4.1e-01    7.1e-04    6.8e-07    7.2e-07
 0.100   6.3e-01    2.2e-01    1.5e-01    1.9e-01
 0.141   7.2e-01    5.5e-01    5.6e-01    1.9e+00
 0.300   8.6e-01    8.4e-01    8.3e-01    4.7e+02
 1.000   9.6e-01    9.6e-01    9.6e-01    2.3e+07

Read the rows. At 0.01 and 0.05 the activations and the slope vanish together, because for small values of tanh a square layer applies the same factor in both directions. At 0.1 they shrink slowly. At 0.141 the activations stay near 0.55 and the slope near 2. At 0.3 and 1 the units are saturated, with a size near 1, the limit of tanh, and the slope explodes by a factor of 470 and of 23 million. Large weights fail in two ways at once: the activations pile up at the ends of tanh, and the slope grows.

How close is close enough?

The factor per layer is raised to the 20th power. A variance factor of 1.1 gives \(1.1^{20} = 6.7\) after 20 layers, a size 2.6 times too large. A factor of 0.9 gives 0.12, a size of 0.35. A factor of 2 gives \(10^{6}\) in variance. Since the factor is proportional to \(\sigma^2\), a spread within about 5% of the right value keeps the variance within 10% per layer. The right band for a deep network is narrow. A default that is close enough for 3 layers can be far off for 20.

Why zeros fail

With all weights 0 the units compute 0. The slope that reaches a layer's weights is the layer's input times a slope that is also 0, so no weight moves. Even if all weights were set to one shared nonzero value, all units in a layer would compute the same number and get the same slope. They would stay identical after all updates (symmetry). A layer of 100 identical units is one unit. Random starting values break the tie. This is why a network starts from random numbers and why the spread of those numbers matters.

The code shows the tie holding. Two hidden units start with the same weights, 0.5 in all positions, and the network trains for 200 steps on Tag 3305. The two rows of \(W^{[1]}\) stay equal. A second run, with slightly different starting rows, ends with different rows.

import numpy as np

x = np.array([0.22, 0.21]); y = 1.0

def train(W1, steps=200, eta=0.5):
    b1, v, c = np.zeros(2), np.array([0.9, 0.9]), 0.0
    for _ in range(steps):
        h = np.tanh(W1 @ x + b1); p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(v @ h + c)))
        d = p - y; d1 = d * v * (1 - h ** 2)
        W1 = W1 - eta * np.outer(d1, x); b1 = b1 - eta * d1; v = v - eta * d * h; c = c - eta * d
    return -np.log(p), W1

loss, W1 = train(np.full((2, 2), 0.5))                          # two identical hidden units
print("equal start:  loss", round(loss, 3), " rows of W1:", W1.round(4).tolist())
loss, W1 = train(np.array([[0.5, 0.4], [0.3, 0.5]]))            # a slightly different start
print("unequal start: loss", round(loss, 3), " rows of W1:", W1.round(4).tolist())
equal start:  loss 0.003  rows of W1: [[0.7525, 0.741], [0.7525, 0.741]]
unequal start: loss 0.003  rows of W1: [[0.7567, 0.645], [0.5594, 0.7476]]

Both runs reach the same loss on this one shark, so the loss does not reveal the problem. With many sharks the second network can learn two different features. The first can learn only one.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Before training, push one batch through the network and print the typical size (the root mean square) of the activations in the layers. If the last layers are near \(10^{-3}\) or \(10^{3}\), fix the initialisation first. In practice, frameworks pick a sensible default for the layer type. This can still go wrong in hand-built or very deep models, or after a change of a layer's width with no change to its initialisation (B8).

More questions

A tanh network has width 100 and weight spread 0.05. About how large are its activations at layer 20?

The variance factor per layer is \(100\times0.05^2 = 0.25\), so the size falls by a factor of 0.5 per layer. After 20 layers that is \(0.5^{20}\approx10^{-6}\). The code above gives \(7\times10^{-7}\).

Choosing the scale: Xavier and He

Guess first. In a network whose layers are 100 units wide, a unit adds up \(n = 100\) inputs, and a good weight spread is about 0.1. You make all layers 4 times wider, so a unit adds up \(n = 400\) inputs. By what factor should the spread change: multiply by 4, by 2, by 1/2 or by 1/4?

To keep the average square of the activations constant, a tanh layer needs the square factor \(n\sigma^2\) of the previous section to equal 1. That gives \(\sigma = 1/\sqrt{n}\), the Xavier spread for a layer with \(n\) inputs and \(n\) outputs. A ReLU sets the negative values to 0, which halves the average square, so a ReLU layer needs \(n\sigma^2/2 = 1\), or \(\sigma = \sqrt{2/n}\), the He spread. The two spreads are proportional to \(1/\sqrt{n}\), so layers 4 times wider need a spread half as large.

  1. The curves come from random networks with made-up weights. Click “width 100” and then “width 400”: the Xavier spread under the plots goes from 0.100 to 0.0500.
  2. Click “width 100” again. With ReLU and the He spread 0.141 the activation size at layer 20 is 0.72. Drag the spread to about 0.047, a third of 0.141, and the size falls to about \(2\times10^{-10}\). Drag it to about 0.43, about three times 0.141, and it rises to about \(3\times10^{9}\). The size factor per layer is applied 20 times.

Going from width 100 to width 400 halves the Xavier spread (0.100 to 0.0500) and the He spread (0.141 to 0.0707), so the answer to the guess is 1/2.

How it works

Take the guess. For \(n = 100\) the tanh rule gives \(\sigma = 1/\sqrt{100} = 0.1\), the value in the question, and the ReLU rule gives \(\sqrt{2/100} = 0.141\). For \(n = 400\) they give \(1/\sqrt{400} = 0.05\) and \(\sqrt{2/400} = 0.0707\), half as large in both cases.

\(\mathrm{Var}(w)\)variance of a starting weight, \(\sigma = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(w)}\)=\(\dfrac{2}{n_{\text{in}} + n_{\text{out}}}\)Xavier: 2/800 = 0.0025, \(\sigma = 0.05\)or\(\dfrac{2}{n_{\text{in}}}\)He: 2/400 = 0.005, \(\sigma = 0.0707\)

Here \(n_{\text{in}}\) is the number of inputs of a unit and \(n_{\text{out}}\) the number of units that its output feeds (both 400). The total input is a sum over \(n_{\text{in}}\) terms, so a tanh layer has the square factor \(n_{\text{in}}\mathrm{Var}(w)\) and needs \(\mathrm{Var}(w) = 1/n_{\text{in}}\). A ReLU halves the average square of a total input that is as often negative as positive, so its square factor is \(n_{\text{in}}\mathrm{Var}(w)/2\) and it needs \(2/n_{\text{in}}\) (He). The slope sent back is a sum of \(n_{\text{out}}\) terms and, for tanh, needs \(1/n_{\text{out}}\). Xavier uses \(2/(n_{\text{in}} + n_{\text{out}})\), a compromise that equals both when \(n_{\text{in}} = n_{\text{out}}\).

Common belief. A single good starting spread works for any network.

Why it fails. The spread has to shrink like \(1/\sqrt{n}\). At width 400 the width-100 He spread 0.141 gives \(n\sigma^2/2 \approx 400 \times 0.02/2 = 4\) for ReLU, so the size doubles per layer. Over 20 layers that is \(2^{20} \approx 10^{6}\) (the figure shows \(7\times10^{5}\)).

Better account. Set the spread from the width of the layer: He for ReLU and Xavier for tanh.

Quick quiz

A ReLU layer has 256 inputs. What is the He spread?

\(\sqrt{2/256} = 0.0884\).

Why does the He rule have a 2 where the tanh rule has a 1?

A ReLU sets the negative values to 0, which halves the average square of its output. A weight variance twice as large compensates for this.

Reading the figure

Switch the width and watch the dip move left as \(n\) grows. The spread must shrink like \(1/\sqrt{n}\), so the guess-first answer is "multiply by 1/2" (\(1/\sqrt{4} = 1/2\)): 0.1 becomes 0.05. Both curves are steep. At width 100 with ReLU, a spread 3 times smaller than the He value (0.047) leaves about \(2\times10^{-10}\) at layer 20, and a spread 3 times larger (0.43) gives about \(3\times10^{9}\), about ten powers of ten in both directions. The band is narrow because the factor is raised to the 20th power.

The vertical lines mark the Xavier spread (dotted) and the He spread (dashed), and the shaded band marks sizes between 0.1 and 10. The 36 spreads were computed offline on random networks, three runs per spread. At width 100, both plots lie inside the band only for spreads from 0.131 to 0.152 with ReLU and from 0.097 to 0.177 with tanh, among the 36 plotted. At width 400 the band contains only 0.072 with ReLU and 0.053 to 0.097 with tanh. A tanh unit cannot output more than 1, so the activation plot of a tanh network stays inside the band at large spreads, but its slope plot leaves the band.

Where the two rules come from

\[ \mathrm{Var}(w) = \frac{2}{n_{\text{in}} + n_{\text{out}}}\ \ \text{(Xavier)}\qquad\qquad \mathrm{Var}(w) = \frac{2}{n_{\text{in}}}\ \ \text{(He)} \]

  • \(\mathrm{Var}(w)\) is the variance of a random starting weight, so the spread is \(\sigma = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(w)}\).
  • \(n_{\text{in}}\) and \(n_{\text{out}}\) are the fan-in and fan-out of the layer. For a square layer \(n_{\text{in}} = n_{\text{out}} = n\) and Xavier gives \(\sigma = 1/\sqrt{n}\).

Forward: the variance factor is \(n_{\text{in}}\mathrm{Var}(w)\) (the calculation of the last section). For tanh near 0 the activation changes little, so the factor should be 1: \(\mathrm{Var}(w) = 1/n_{\text{in}}\). A ReLU keeps the positive half of a distribution that is symmetric around 0. The square \(z^2\) is the same for \(z\) and \(-z\), so half of \(\mathbb{E}[z^2]\) comes from the positive values, and \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ReLU}(z)^2] = \tfrac12 \mathbb{E}[z^2]\). The factor becomes \(n_{\text{in}}\mathrm{Var}(w)/2\), and setting it to 1 gives \(\mathrm{Var}(w) = 2/n_{\text{in}}\), the He rule. Backward: the slope sent to a layer's inputs is \(W^\top\boldsymbol\delta\) (B4). It is a sum over \(n_{\text{out}}\) terms \(\delta_i W_{ij}\), independent with mean 0 as before. Its variance factor is \(n_{\text{out}}\mathrm{Var}(w)\), and a factor of 1 needs \(\mathrm{Var}(w) = 1/n_{\text{out}}\). The forward rule wants \(1/n_{\text{in}}\), the backward rule \(1/n_{\text{out}}\). Xavier takes \(2/(n_{\text{in}} + n_{\text{out}})\), which is the harmonic mean of \(1/n_{\text{in}}\) and \(1/n_{\text{out}}\) (it equals both when \(n_{\text{in}} = n_{\text{out}}\)).

A second worked example

variance 2 ÷ (100 + 50)Xavier, 100 in, 50 out=0.0133spread 0.115|variance 2 ÷ 100He=0.02spread 0.141|√(6 ÷ 150)Xavier bound if uniform=0.2weights in −0.2 to 0.2

The box is a second worked example, for a layer with 100 inputs and 50 outputs. The last cell uses the uniform version of Xavier: weights drawn evenly from \(-a\) to \(a\) have variance \(a^2/3\), so \(a = \sqrt{6/(n_{\text{in}}+n_{\text{out}})}\) gives variance \(2/(n_{\text{in}}+n_{\text{out}})\). Some libraries draw from this uniform range and some from a normal distribution with the same variance.

A wider layer

Move to width 400, the guess-first case. The He spread is \(\sqrt{2/400} = 0.071\), and the Xavier spread for a square layer is \(1/\sqrt{400} = 0.05\). Suppose the width-100 value 0.1 is kept by mistake. For tanh the variance factor becomes \(400\times0.01 = 4\), so the signal would double per layer. Tanh cannot exceed 1, so the units saturate and the slopes grow instead. For ReLU the factor is \(4/2 = 2\), the size grows by \(\sqrt2\) per layer, and \(2^{10}\approx10^{3}\) after 20 layers.

Layers that are not dense

A convolution (C1) adds up channels times the filter's height times its width inputs. For a \(3\times3\) filter over 64 channels the fan-in is \(64\times9 = 576\), and the fan-out of 128 filters is \(128\times9 = 1152\). The He spread is \(\sqrt{2/576} = 0.059\). The same weight is used at many positions, but the variance depends on the number of terms in one sum, and that is the fan-in. The code checks the formulas against PyTorch's initialisers.

import torch, torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
conv = nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernel_size=3)           # 64 input channels, 128 filters of size 3 by 3
fan_in, fan_out = 64 * 3 * 3, 128 * 3 * 3
print("fan-in:", fan_in, " fan-out:", fan_out)
nn.init.kaiming_normal_(conv.weight, nonlinearity="relu")
print("He spread: formula", round((2 / fan_in) ** 0.5, 4), " measured", round(conv.weight.std().item(), 4))
nn.init.xavier_normal_(conv.weight)
print("Xavier spread: formula", round((2 / (fan_in + fan_out)) ** 0.5, 4), " measured", round(conv.weight.std().item(), 4))
fan-in: 576  fan-out: 1152
He spread: formula 0.0589  measured 0.059
Xavier spread: formula 0.034  measured 0.0341

Where this stops being right

The derivation assumes independent weights with mean 0 and inputs of a steady size, and it treats the activation as linear (tanh) or as a clean half (ReLU). Actual tanh units saturate when inputs are large, so the figure's tanh curve shows the signal shrinking by a factor of about 6 to 7 even at Xavier. After training starts, weights are no longer random. Normalisation layers (next section) make the starting scale matter much less. In practice, use He for ReLU-type activations and Xavier for tanh and sigmoid, and trust the library defaults unless you change the width or the activation. PyTorch's default for nn.Linear is a uniform draw with variance \(1/(3\,n_{\text{in}})\), which the code below confirms. A common mistake is to copy the spread of a narrow layer into a wide one.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, depth = 100, 20
x0 = rng.standard_normal((256, n))                      # inputs of typical size 1

def run(sigma):
    x = x0
    for _ in range(depth):
        W = rng.standard_normal((n, n)) * sigma         # one layer: random weights with spread sigma
        x = np.maximum(0, x @ W)                        # ReLU
    return np.sqrt((x ** 2).mean())

for name, s in [("too small", 0.01), ("Xavier", np.sqrt(2 / (n + n))), ("He", np.sqrt(2 / n)), ("too large", 1.0)]:
    print(f"{name:9s} spread {s:.3f}: size at layer 20 = {run(s):.1e}")
too small spread 0.010: size at layer 20 = 5.4e-24
Xavier    spread 0.100: size at layer 20 = 5.4e-04
He        spread 0.141: size at layer 20 = 2.4e+00
too large spread 1.000: size at layer 20 = 9.8e+16

Xavier's spread on a ReLU network loses a factor of \(2\) in variance per layer, \(2^{20} \approx 10^{6}\) after 20 layers, which is a size of \(10^{-3}\) as the output shows. The same weights through PyTorch's own initialisers:

import torch, torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
layer = nn.Linear(100, 100)
print("PyTorch default spread:      ", round(layer.weight.std().item(), 4), "  (1/sqrt(3*100) =", round((1 / (3 * 100)) ** 0.5, 4), ")")
nn.init.kaiming_normal_(layer.weight, nonlinearity="relu")
print("kaiming_normal_ spread:      ", round(layer.weight.std().item(), 4), "  (sqrt(2/100) =", round((2 / 100) ** 0.5, 4), ")")
nn.init.xavier_normal_(layer.weight)
print("xavier_normal_ spread:       ", round(layer.weight.std().item(), 4), "  (sqrt(2/200) =", round((2 / 200) ** 0.5, 4), ")")
nn.init.zeros_(layer.bias)
PyTorch default spread:       0.0576   (1/sqrt(3*100) = 0.0577 )
kaiming_normal_ spread:       0.1438   (sqrt(2/100) = 0.1414 )
xavier_normal_ spread:        0.1002   (sqrt(2/200) = 0.1 )

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a hand-made network trains in one width and not in another, print the activation size per layer in both. The mismatch is often a spread that did not change with the width. Biases are often started at 0 (the default layers of PyTorch start them at small random values), which causes no symmetry problem because the weights are random.

Where this is used

Used in: the starting-loss check (B8), the layer-size checks (B8) and the residual and normalisation choices of the next two sections.

More questions

A convolution with ReLU has \(3\times3\) filters over 32 input channels. What is the He spread?

The fan-in is \(32\times9 = 288\), so the spread is \(\sqrt{2/288} = 1/12 = 0.083\).

Normalisation

Guess first. In the grid below (made-up values), rows are the 6 sharks of a batch and columns are the 8 hidden units of one layer. Layer norm averages a set of cells together. Is that set a column (one hidden unit across the sharks) or a row (all hidden units of one shark)? Does batch norm use the same set?

A normalisation layer rescales a set of numbers to mean 0 and variance 1. It subtracts their mean \(\mu\), divides by their standard deviation, and then applies a learned scale \(\gamma\) and shift \(\beta\). Batch norm, layer norm and group norm use this one formula. They differ in one choice, which cells form the set: a column for batch norm, a row for layer norm and part of a row for group norm. RMS norm is layer norm without the mean subtraction. It divides by the root mean square of the row (the square root of its average square) and has no shift \(\beta\).

  1. Choose “Layer norm” and “After normalising”. The outlined cells, the set that shares one mean and one variance, form a row, and the thickly outlined cell, Tag 3305 with h3, becomes +0.82. With “Batch norm” it becomes −1.36.
  2. With “Batch norm”, drag “Sharks in the batch” from 6 down to 2: the cell becomes −1.00, while with layer norm it stays +0.82.

Layer norm gives Tag 3305, h3 the same +0.82 whatever else is in the batch; batch norm, which uses the batch, gives −1.36 with six sharks and −1.00 with two.

How it works

Take Tag 3305, h3, with value 1.6. Batch norm uses the six values in the column of h3, which have mean 3.38 and variance 1.72, so \(\hat x = (1.6 - 3.38)/\sqrt{1.72} = -1.36\). Layer norm uses the eight values in the row of Tag 3305, which have mean 0.30 and variance 2.50, so \(\hat x = (1.6 - 0.30)/\sqrt{2.50} = +0.82\).

\(\hat x\)normalised value: −1.36=(\(x\)the cell: 1.6−\(\mu\)mean of the set: 3.38)÷\(\sqrt{\mathrm{var}+\epsilon}\)standard deviation of the set: 1.31→\(y = \gamma\hat x + \beta\)output: −1.36 for \(\gamma = 1\), \(\beta = 0\)

The variance of a set is the average of the squared differences from its mean. The constant \(\epsilon\) (\(10^{-5}\) in PyTorch) keeps the division safe when the variance is 0. The learned \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) start at 1 and 0 and can change in training, so the layer can learn another scale and shift. A layer then receives numbers at a scale set by \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\), whatever the weights before it did. This usually keeps the activations and slopes in range (why it helps is still debated).

Common belief. Normalisation treats a shark on its own, so its output depends only on that shark.

Why it fails. Batch norm in training mode uses the other sharks in the batch, so a shark's output changes with its neighbours. At test time it uses stored averages, the means and variances recorded during training.

Better account. Layer, RMS and group norm use only the shark's own row. For testing, switch a batch-norm model to evaluation mode (model.eval() in PyTorch).

Quick quiz

Layer-normalise the row \((1, 3, 5, 7)\), taking \(\epsilon = 0\), \(\gamma = 1\) and \(\beta = 0\).

The mean is 4 and the variance is \((9 + 1 + 1 + 9)/4 = 5\), so the standard deviation is 2.236. The result is \((-1.342, -0.447, 0.447, 1.342)\).

What does batch norm do with a batch of one shark in training mode, and why?

A hidden unit has a single value, so its variance is 0 and \(x - \mu = 0\). The normalised value is then 0 for all cells (\(\epsilon\) keeps the division defined) and the output equals \(\beta\). PyTorch's BatchNorm1d raises an error instead, as the code under Go deeper shows.

Terms

normalisation
shifting and scaling a set of numbers so that they have mean 0 and variance 1, then applying a learned scale \(\gamma\) and shift \(\beta\)
batch norm
normalises a hidden unit over the sharks of the batch
layer norm
normalises a shark over all of its hidden units
RMS norm
layer norm without subtracting the mean: divides by the root mean square
group norm
layer norm within a few groups of hidden units

Reading the figure

The values are made up: hidden values for six sharks, with the hidden units on their own scales.

Click any cell. The outlined cells share one mean and one variance. Choose a norm and see its set: a column for batch norm, a row for layer norm and RMS norm, a part of a row for group norm. Then press "After normalising": in the outlined set the mean is 0 and the variance is 1 (RMS norm instead has root mean square 1, and batch norm with stored averages has neither). The equation boxes work the chosen cell through step by step. Try these: slide the batch down to one shark with batch norm selected; then switch to "Stored averages (test time)".

The formulas

\[ \hat x = \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\mathrm{var} + \epsilon}},\qquad y = \gamma\,\hat x + \beta \qquad\qquad \hat x = \frac{x}{\sqrt{\mathrm{mean}(x^2) + \epsilon}},\qquad y = \gamma\,\hat x\ \ \text{(RMS norm)} \]

  • \(\mu\) and \(\mathrm{var}\) are the mean and variance of the cells in the set (0.7). \(\epsilon\) is a tiny constant (PyTorch uses \(10^{-5}\)) that keeps the division safe when the variance is 0.
  • \(\hat x\) is the normalised value. \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) are learned numbers, one pair per hidden unit. For batch norm, setting \(\gamma = \sqrt{\mathrm{var}}\) and \(\beta = \mu\) would undo the normalisation, so the layer can keep the original scale if training moves \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) there.

Why the result has mean 0 and variance 1

The numerator \(x - \mu\) sums to 0 over the set, so the mean of \(\hat x\) is 0. Its mean square is \(\mathrm{mean}[(x-\mu)^2]/(\mathrm{var} + \epsilon) = \mathrm{var}/(\mathrm{var}+\epsilon)\), which is 1 up to \(\epsilon\). A worked example by hand, with the row \((1, 3, 5, 7)\): the mean is 4, the variance is \((9 + 1 + 1 + 9)/4 = 5\), the standard deviation 2.236, and the normalised row is \((-1.342, -0.447, 0.447, 1.342)\). RMS norm of the same row divides by \(\sqrt{(1 + 9 + 25 + 49)/4} = \sqrt{21} = 4.583\) and gives \((0.218, 0.655, 1.091, 1.528)\): its mean is 0.873, not 0, and its root mean square is 1. The code below prints both and compares with PyTorch.

import numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn

x = np.array([[1.0, 3.0, 5.0, 7.0]])                  # one shark, four hidden values
mu, var = x.mean(), x.var()                           # statistics of this one row
ln = (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + 1e-5)                   # layer norm, scale 1 and shift 0
rms = x / np.sqrt((x ** 2).mean() + 1e-5)             # RMS norm, scale 1
print("layer norm:", ln.round(3), " mean", ln.mean().round(3), " var", ln.var().round(3))
print("RMS norm:  ", rms.round(3), " mean", rms.mean().round(3), " rms", np.sqrt((rms ** 2).mean()).round(3))

t = torch.tensor(x, dtype=torch.float32)
print("torch LayerNorm:", nn.LayerNorm(4)(t).detach().numpy().round(3), " eps =", nn.LayerNorm(4).eps)
bn = nn.BatchNorm1d(4)
print("BatchNorm1d eps =", bn.eps, " momentum =", bn.momentum)
try:
    bn.train(); bn(t)
except ValueError as e:
    print("batch of one in training mode:", e)
layer norm: [[-1.342 -0.447  0.447  1.342]]  mean 0.0  var 1.0
RMS norm:   [[0.218 0.655 1.091 1.528]]  mean 0.873  rms 1.0
torch LayerNorm: [[-1.342 -0.447  0.447  1.342]]  eps = 1e-05
BatchNorm1d eps = 1e-05  momentum = 0.1
batch of one in training mode: Expected more than 1 value per channel when training, got input size torch.Size([1, 4])

Scale, shift and groups in numbers

Take the normalised row \((-1.342, -0.447, 0.447, 1.342)\) and learned values \(\gamma = 2\) and \(\beta = 0.5\). The output is \(2\times(-1.342) + 0.5 = -2.18\), then \(-0.39\), \(1.39\) and \(3.18\): mean 0.5 and spread 2. Training can move \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) away from 1 and 0 when another scale lowers the loss.

Groups change which cells share statistics. Take a row of 8 values, \((1, 3, 5, 7)\) followed by \((2, 4, 6, 8)\), where the second half is shifted up by 1. Layer norm treats the row as one set, so the shift remains as a difference of 0.44 between the halves. Group norm with two groups normalises the halves separately, so both become the same row. The code prints both.

import numpy as np

row = np.array([1.0, 3.0, 5.0, 7.0, 2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0])        # two halves; the second is shifted up by 1
norm = lambda a: (a - a.mean()) / np.sqrt(a.var() + 1e-5)

print("layer norm: ", norm(row).round(3).tolist())
print("group norm: ", np.concatenate([norm(row[:4]), norm(row[4:])]).round(3).tolist())
gamma, beta = 2.0, 0.5
print("layer norm of the first half, with gamma 2 and beta 0.5:", (gamma * norm(row[:4]) + beta).round(3).tolist())
layer norm:  [-1.528, -0.655, 0.218, 1.091, -1.091, -0.218, 0.655, 1.528]
group norm:  [-1.342, -0.447, 0.447, 1.342, -1.342, -0.447, 0.447, 1.342]
layer norm of the first half, with gamma 2 and beta 0.5: [-2.183, -0.394, 1.394, 3.183]

Why normalising helps

A layer then receives inputs at a scale set by the learned \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\), whatever the weights before it did. The signal usually does not drift to 0 or to huge values, and the slopes of B4 usually stay in range. Normalisation often allows a larger learning rate and makes the starting scale matter less. It is the same idea as standardising the inputs of A2, applied to the hidden values inside the network. The original batch-norm paper explained the benefit as a reduction of "internal covariate shift", the change in a layer's input distribution during training. Whether that is the reason is debated (Santurkar and others, 2018, argue against this account), so treat the effect as better established than the mechanism.

The differences, with numbers

Take the figure's default cell, Tag 3305 and \(h_3\), with value 1.6. Batch norm uses the six values in its column: mean 3.38, variance 1.72, so \(\hat x = (1.6 - 3.38)/1.31 = -1.36\). Layer norm uses the eight values in its row: mean 0.30, variance 2.50, so \(\hat x = (1.6 - 0.30)/1.58 = +0.82\). The same cell becomes negative under one norm and positive under the other, because it is compared with different cells. Layer norm does not change when the other sharks change. Group norm uses 4 of the 8 values (2 groups) or 2 (4 groups). It is a middle way, useful when a batch is too small for batch norm and the features are too varied for one shared mean. Batch norm in training mode uses the batch statistics. At test time a single shark has no batch. The layer uses stored averages kept during training as an exponential moving average (0.7), with PyTorch's default momentum 0.1. The figure shows these stored values below the grid.

A third answer for the same cell. Switch the figure to "Stored averages (test time)". For \(h_3\) the stored mean is 2.01 and the stored variance 4.29, kept from 80 more made-up sharks. The cell becomes \((1.6 - 2.01)/\sqrt{4.29} = -0.20\). That is a third value for the same number, and it is the one the layer uses at test time. The batch of six had mean 3.38 and variance 1.72. Six sharks gave a mean that is off by 1.4 and a variance that is 2.5 times too small, which shows how noisy the statistics of a small batch can be.

The code below trains a batch-norm layer on batches with mean about 5 and spread 2, then normalises the same shark next to two different neighbours. In evaluation mode the answer does not change. In training mode the neighbour sets the answer: with two values in the batch the shark can only come out as \(-1\) or \(+1\).

import torch, torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
bn = nn.BatchNorm1d(1)
for _ in range(300):
    bn(torch.randn(16, 1) * 2 + 5)                  # training batches: values around 5, spread 2
mean, var = bn.running_mean.item(), bn.running_var.item()
print("stored mean", round(mean, 2), " stored variance", round(var, 2))

shark = torch.tensor([[6.0]])
bn.eval()                                           # evaluation mode: use the stored averages
for neighbour in (7.0, 1.0):
    out = bn(torch.cat([shark, torch.tensor([[neighbour]])]))[0].item()
    print(f"eval mode,  neighbour {neighbour}: shark -> {out:.3f}")
print("by hand, (6 - mean) / sqrt(var + eps) =", round((6 - mean) / (var + 1e-5) ** 0.5, 3))
bn.train()                                          # training mode: use the batch of two
for neighbour in (7.0, 1.0):
    out = bn(torch.cat([shark, torch.tensor([[neighbour]])]))[0].item()
    print(f"train mode, neighbour {neighbour}: shark -> {out:.3f}")
stored mean 5.0  stored variance 3.81
eval mode,  neighbour 7.0: shark -> 0.513
eval mode,  neighbour 1.0: shark -> 0.513
by hand, (6 - mean) / sqrt(var + eps) = 0.513
train mode, neighbour 7.0: shark -> -1.000
train mode, neighbour 1.0: shark -> 1.000

What a norm layer adds

PyTorch starts \(\gamma\) at 1 and \(\beta\) at 0, so a new norm layer begins as plain standardising. A layer norm over 512 features has 1,024 learned numbers, one \(\gamma\) and one \(\beta\) per feature. Batch norm has the same 1,024 and also stores a running mean and a running variance per feature. Those 1,024 stored numbers are updated while the model trains and are not learned by gradient descent.

Where they break

Batch norm needs a batch bigger than 1, and its error grows as the batch shrinks (Wu and He, 2018). The stored averages can also differ from the statistics of new data, which is one more way a model can fail when the water changes (C3). Layer norm does not depend on the batch and is the usual choice for text, where a token is normalised on its own (D5). RMS norm drops the mean subtraction. Zhang and Sennrich (2019) report that it works about as well as layer norm and is cheaper, with 7% to 64% less running time in their models. In practice, use batch norm for image networks with ordinary batch sizes, group norm when the batch is small, and layer norm or RMS norm for sequences. A common mistake is forgetting model.eval(): the layer then keeps using batch statistics at test time, and one shark's answer changes with its neighbours.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a model works in training and gives odd outputs on a single test image, check that it is in evaluation mode and that the stored averages were updated. PyTorch raises an error for a batch of one in training mode, as above. If outputs for the same shark differ between runs with different batches, a batch statistic is leaking in.

More questions

Which of batch, layer, RMS and group norm give a shark the same output whatever else is in the batch?

Layer norm, RMS norm and group norm, because a shark's cells are normalised using only that shark's own row. Batch norm in training mode uses the other sharks.

A row has two halves, \((1, 3, 5, 7)\) and \((2, 4, 6, 8)\). Which of layer norm and two-group norm keeps the difference between the halves?

Layer norm keeps it. The second half comes out 0.44 higher than the first. Group norm normalises the two halves separately, so they become the same row and the difference is gone.

Residual connections

Guess first. A stack has 30 plain blocks, which are layers of 64 tanh units with random weights of scale 0.6 (spread 0.6/\(\sqrt{64}\) = 0.075). A block outputs \(F(x)\) for its input \(x\) and multiplies the slope that goes back through it by about 0.6. The slope (the gradient of the loss) reaching block 0, the block nearest the input, is a tiny fraction of the slope at the output. If all blocks output \(x + F(x)\) instead, how much does that slope change: about the same, ten times larger, or more than a million times larger?

A residual connection, or shortcut, adds a block's input to its output: \(y = x + F(x)\), where \(F\) is what the plain block computes. The slope arriving at \(y\) reaches \(x\) along two paths, one through \(F\) and one straight through the shortcut, which leaves the slope unchanged. So at a block, the part of the slope that takes the shortcut is not multiplied by the block slope \(\partial F/\partial x\).

  1. The weights are random and made up. The bars show the slope size block by block, with the output's slope as 1 on a log axis. Without shortcuts the bar at block 0 is \(1.5\times10^{-7}\); click “With residual connections” and it becomes 6.0.
  2. Drag the weight scale to 1.0: the readout under the plot gives the slope at block 0 as 0.16 without shortcuts and 13 with them.

At weight scale 0.6 the slope reaching block 0 is \(1.5\times10^{-7}\) of the output's without shortcuts and 6.0 times it with them: more than a million times larger.

How it works

Take a toy chain of 30 blocks that map one number to one number, with block slope \(\partial F/\partial x = 0.1\), and an arriving slope of 1. At one block the slope reaching its input is \(1 \times (1 + 0.1) = 1.1\) with the shortcut and \(1 \times 0.1 = 0.1\) without. After 30 blocks these become \(1.1^{30} = 17.4\) and \(0.1^{30} = 10^{-30}\). In the figure at weight scale 0.6 the measured factor per block is 0.59 without shortcuts and 1.06 with them.

\(\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial x}\)slope reaching the input: 1.1=\(\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial y}\)slope arriving at the output: 1×(\(I\)the shortcut leaves the slope unchanged: 1+\(\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial x}\)the block slope: 0.1)

The slope reaching block 0 is a sum over paths that take the shortcut or go through \(F\) at a block. The path through all the shortcuts multiplies the slope by 1 whatever the depth, so that term does not shrink. Other paths add to it and can make it grow, as the figure shows at weight scale 1.0.

Common belief. A shortcut only adds a copy of the input, so it cannot change how well training works.

Why it fails. The shortcut gives the slope a direct path back, as the figure shows at weight scale 0.6.

Better account. The shortcut adds a second path to the sum of paths in backpropagation. It also lets activations and slopes grow. Deep stacks often add normalisation or small last-layer weights as well (see Go deeper).

Quick quiz

Why is the slope through a residual block a sum of two terms?

The block's input \(x\) is used twice: it is added directly to the output and it also goes into \(F\). A value used twice gets the sum of the slopes along both paths, \(I\) and \(\partial F/\partial x\).

In the toy chain of 30 blocks, the block slope is \(-0.1\) instead of \(+0.1\). What slope reaches block 0 with shortcuts?

The factor per block is \(1 - 0.1 = 0.9\), and \(0.9^{30} = 0.042\). A slightly negative block slope shrinks the slope slowly, and about 4% of it is left after 30 blocks. Without shortcuts the result would be \((-0.1)^{30}\), about \(10^{-30}\) in size.

Terms

residual connection
a shortcut that adds a block's input to its output: \(y = x + F(x)\)
block
one stage of the network, here a layer with an activation, written \(F\)
identity path
the shortcut route through the network that skips the blocks

Reading the figure

The blocks are random tanh layers of width 64 with made-up weights, at weight scale 0.6 unless you move the slider (1.0 is the Xavier scale for tanh).

Toggle the switch and watch the bars at the left of the plot, the blocks nearest the input. The dotted line keeps the other setting visible. Then raise the weight scale to 1. The plain stack now passes on more of the slope (0.16 of the output's), while the shortcut stack grows (13 times the output's). The shortcut brings the other problem with it, and the readout below the plot shows the activations growing too.

The formulas

\[ \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x} + F(\mathbf{x}) \qquad\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{y}}\Big(I + \frac{\partial F}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\Big) \]

  • \(F\) is what the block computes (a weight matrix and an activation). \(I\) is the identity: the slope passed straight through the shortcut.
  • \(\partial F/\partial\mathbf{x}\) is the slope of the block. In the right-hand formula the two terms are the two paths of B4: through the shortcut (the \(I\)) and through the block.

Why the slope persists

A block \(y = x + F(x)\) uses \(x\) twice, so by the sum rule of B4 the slope to \(x\) is the sum of two paths. Through \(L\) blocks the slope picks up a product \(\prod_l (I + J_l)\) with \(J_l = \partial F_l/\partial \mathbf{x}\). Multiply out the product: it contains the term \(I\) (all shortcuts), plus terms with one or more \(J_l\). The identity term does not shrink with depth. In a plain stack the slope is the product \(\prod_l J_l\) alone, which is the chain of small factors of B4. With scalar numbers and 30 blocks, the slope reaching block 0 passes 30 factors, one per block. If a block's slope is \(f = 0.8\), a plain stack gives \(0.8^{30} \approx 0.0012\) (the 30 layers of the ReLU example of B4 have 29 factors between their ends, and gave \(0.8^{29} \approx 0.0015\)). With a shortcut the factor per block is \(1 + f\); for a block slope of \(+0.05\) it gives \(1.05^{30} \approx 4.3\), and for \(-0.05\) it gives \(0.95^{30} \approx 0.21\). The shortcut keeps the factor near 1 when the blocks are gentle.

plain: 0.830 ≈ 0.0012block slope 0.8|shortcuts: 1.0530 ≈ 4.3block slope +0.05|shortcuts: 0.9530 ≈ 0.21block slope −0.05

Two blocks by hand

Let two blocks have slopes \(f_1 = 0.1\) and \(f_2 = 0.2\). With shortcuts the slope through both is \((1+0.1)(1+0.2) = 1.32\). Multiply it out: \(1 + 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.02\). The 1 is the path through both shortcuts. The 0.1 and 0.2 are the paths through one block only, and 0.02 is the path through both blocks. A plain stack has only the last term, 0.02, which is 66 times smaller than 1.32. With 30 blocks there are \(2^{30}\) paths, and the one that skips all blocks always has the weight 1.

two blocks:1.1 × 1.2(1 + f1)(1 + f2)=1both shortcuts+0.1block 1 only+0.2block 2 only+0.02both blocks, the only term a plain stack keeps

In NumPy

The code builds the figure's setting in NumPy: width 64, 30 blocks and weight scale 0.6. Its random numbers differ from the figure's, so the digits differ a little (the figure shows \(1.5\times10^{-7}\) without shortcuts and 6.0 with them). Over 40 other seeds the slope without shortcuts ranged from \(7\times10^{-8}\) to \(2.4\times10^{-7}\) and with shortcuts from 5.2 to 6.9, so the figure's numbers are typical. Without shortcuts both the activations and the slope are tiny. With shortcuts the slope is larger than at the output, and the activations have grown too.

import numpy as np

n, depth, batch, scale = 64, 30, 16, 0.6            # width, blocks, sharks, weight scale of a block
rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
Ws = [rng.standard_normal((n, n)) * scale / np.sqrt(n) for _ in range(depth)]
x0 = rng.standard_normal((batch, n)); g_out = rng.standard_normal((batch, n))
size = lambda a: np.linalg.norm(a, axis=1).mean()

for residual in (False, True):
    h, zs = x0, []
    for W in Ws:
        z = h @ W; zs.append(z)
        h = np.tanh(z) + (h if residual else 0)         # a block: tanh(Wh), plus the shortcut if on
    g = g_out
    for W, z in zip(reversed(Ws), reversed(zs)):
        g = (g * (1 - np.tanh(z) ** 2)) @ W.T + (g if residual else 0)
    print(f"residual {str(residual):5s}: slope at block 0 = {size(g) / size(g_out):.1e} of the output slope, activation size {np.sqrt((h ** 2).mean()):.1e}")
residual False: slope at block 0 = 1.9e-07 of the output slope, activation size 1.9e-07
residual True : slope at block 0 = 5.8e+00 of the output slope, activation size 4.2e+00

Where it breaks

The activations also add up, so with blocks of gain near 1 the size of \(x\) grows with depth, and the slope can grow too (the figure shows this at larger weight scales). Deep residual networks therefore often combine shortcuts with normalisation layers or with small starting weights in the last layer of a block (D5 shows the arrangement in a transformer block). The shortcut also needs \(x\) and \(F(x)\) to have the same size. When a block changes the width, the shortcut passes through a small learned layer instead, called a projection. Going from 64 to 128 channels with a \(1\times1\) projection costs \(64\times128 = 8{,}192\) weights. He and others (2016) reported that residual learning made much deeper networks easier to optimise, up to 152 layers on ImageNet. In practice, nearly all very deep networks (image models with tens or hundreds of layers, and transformers) use residual connections. A common mistake is a shortcut that adds tensors of different sizes, which fails loudly, or one that skips the normalisation and lets the scale drift.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a very deep plain stack does not train at all, add the shortcuts before changing anything else, and check the activation size at the last block. If the loss becomes NaN soon after, the activations are growing: lower the block weights or add normalisation.

More questions

All 30 blocks of a residual stack have slope \(+0.1\). What is the slope reaching block 0, compared with the output?

\(1.1^{30} \approx 17.4\). The slope grows, which is why shortcuts need small blocks or normalisation.

Dropout

Guess first. During training you switch off a hidden unit with probability 0.5, and at test time you switch none off. Suppose you made no other change. Would the total input to a unit of the next layer be about the same at test time as in training, about twice as large, or about half?

In dropout, a training step sets hidden units to 0 at random: a given unit is set to 0 with probability \(p\), independently of the others. The network that trains is then a random sub-network that changes from step to step. In most libraries the kept units are multiplied by \(1/(1-p)\). This keeps the average total input to the next layer equal to its value in the full network, where no unit is dropped. At test time all units are kept and no scaling is needed.

  1. The network and its weights are made up. Press “Resample the mask” a few times: a mask is the random choice of which hidden units are dropped (crossed circles), and the output changes with it.
  2. The histogram shows the total input to one unit over 2,000 masks. Its mean, the dashed coral line, is 1.27, near the navy line, the full network's 1.28; choose “No scaling” and the mean falls to 0.63, about half.

With the scaling the mean total input is 1.27 against 1.28 at test time; without it, 0.63, so the test-time input would be twice that of training.

How it works

Take a unit with value \(a = 0.8\) and \(p = 0.5\). If the unit is kept its output is \(0.8/(1-0.5) = 1.6\), and if it is dropped its output is 0, both with probability 0.5. The mean output is \(0.5 \times 1.6 + 0.5 \times 0 = 0.8\), which is \(a\), and the variance is \(0.5 \times (1.6-0.8)^2 + 0.5 \times (0-0.8)^2 = 0.64\).

\(\tilde a\)output after dropout: 1.6 or 0=\(m\)mask: 1 with probability \(1-p\), else 0×\(a\)value of the unit: 0.8÷\(1-p\)0.5→\(a\)mean: 0.8|\(a^2\dfrac{p}{1-p}\)variance: 0.64

Without the factor \(1/(1-p)\) the mean would be \((1-p)\,a\), half of \(a\) at \(p = 0.5\). The total input to a unit of the next layer is a weighted sum of such outputs, so its mean over many masks equals the full network's value. Dropout adds noise with variance \(a^2p/(1-p)\), which equals \(a^2\) at \(p = 0.5\). Dropout is used to reduce overfitting, the case where a network does much better on its training data than on new data. A common explanation is that a unit cannot rely on a partner being present.

Analogy. Dropout resembles training a team of many small networks, made of random subsets of the units, and averaging their answers at test time. The original dropout paper (Srivastava and others, 2014) describes dropout this way.

Where it breaks. The sub-networks are not independent models. They share all their weights, and the full network only approximates the average of their predictions.

Quick quiz

Why multiply the kept units by \(1/(1-p)\) during training?

To keep the average total input to the next layer equal to what the full network produces at test time. Without it, the next layer would receive about \((1-p)\) times the test-time input during training.

With \(p = 0.2\) and a unit value of 1.0, what are the mean and variance of the unit's output?

Mean 1.0. Variance \(1.0^2 \times 0.2/0.8 = 0.25\).

Go deeper algebra, all masks, code, practice, debug tip about 6 min

Terms

dropout
setting a random share \(p\) of the hidden units to 0 on a training step
mask
the random 0-or-1 choice for a unit on one step
inverted dropout
multiplying the kept units by \(1/(1-p)\) during training, so that no change is needed at test time
thinned network
the smaller network that is left after a mask removes some units

Reading the figure

The network has made-up random weights, and its output is the chance that the shark is an adult. The diagram is the same network as the one behind the histogram.

Press "Resample the mask" a few times. A press switches off a different set of hidden units (dashed circles with a cross), and the output changes with it. The histogram shows the total input to one unit of the second hidden layer over 2,000 masks. The dashed coral line is its mean and the navy line is its value in the full network at test time. Switch the scaling off and the mean drops to about half of the navy line, because the kept units no longer make up for the dropped ones. The answer to the guess-first question follows: without scaling the test-time input is about twice the training input. With 12 hidden units there are \(2^{12} = 4096\) possible masks (0.4), so one network trains as a very large set of sub-networks that share their weights.

The formulas

\[ \tilde a_i = \frac{m_i\, a_i}{1-p},\qquad m_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(1-p) \qquad\qquad \mathbb{E}[\tilde a_i] = a_i,\quad \mathrm{Var}[\tilde a_i] = a_i^2\,\frac{p}{1-p} \]

  • \(a_i\) is the value of hidden unit \(i\) and \(m_i\) its mask: 1 (kept) with probability \(1-p\), 0 (dropped) with probability \(p\). \(\tilde a_i\) is the value passed on in training.
  • At test time \(m_i\) is always 1 and the factor \(1/(1-p)\) is left out, so the full network uses \(a_i\) itself.

Why the average is right

With probability \(1-p\) the unit passes \(a/(1-p)\), and with probability \(p\) it passes 0. The mean is \((1-p)\cdot\tfrac{a}{1-p} + p\cdot 0 = a\). The variance is \((1-p)\big(\tfrac{a}{1-p} - a\big)^2 + p\,a^2 = a^2\tfrac{p^2}{1-p} + p\,a^2 = a^2\tfrac{p}{1-p}\), the noise that dropout adds. Take a unit with \(a = 0.8\). With \(p = 0.5\) it passes 1.6 half the time and 0 half the time: mean 0.8, variance \(0.64 = 0.8^2\). With \(p = 0.1\) it passes 0.889 nine times in ten and 0 once in ten: mean 0.8, variance \(0.8^2 \times 0.1/0.9 = 0.071\). A small \(p\) adds little noise, and \(p = 0.5\) adds noise whose variance equals \(a^2\). The code confirms 0.8 and 0.64 on 10,000 draws. The total input to a unit in the next layer is a weighted sum of such values, so its mean is also unchanged, which is what the figure shows.

import torch, torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(1)
drop = nn.Dropout(p=0.5)
a = torch.full((8,), 0.8)
print("training:", drop(a))
print("training:", drop(a))
drop.eval()
print("eval:    ", drop(a))
drop.train()
many = torch.stack([drop(a) for _ in range(10000)])
print("mean of 10000 training outputs:", many.mean().round(decimals=3).item(), " variance:", many.var().round(decimals=3).item())

eval:     tensor([0.8000, 0.8000, 0.8000, 0.8000, 0.8000, 0.8000, 0.8000, 0.8000])

All the masks of a tiny layer

Take three hidden values \(a = (0.8, 0.5, 0.3)\) with weights \((1.0, -0.6, 0.9)\) into one unit of the next layer. At test time the input is \(0.8 - 0.3 + 0.27 = 0.77\). With \(p = 0.5\) there are \(2^3 = 8\) masks, and a kept value is doubled. The code lists the input for all eight. They run from \(-0.6\) to 2.14. The mean is 0.77, the test-time value, and without the doubling it would be 0.385. The spread across masks is 0.90, larger than the signal. That spread is the noise that dropout adds, and the network has to give good answers despite it.

import itertools, numpy as np

a = np.array([0.8, 0.5, 0.3])                        # three hidden values
w = np.array([1.0, -0.6, 0.9])                       # their weights into one unit of the next layer
print("test-time input:", round(a @ w, 3))

p = 0.5; totals = []
for mask in itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=3):     # all 8 masks, equally likely
    totals.append((np.array(mask) * a / (1 - p)) @ w)
totals = np.array(totals)
print("inputs over the 8 masks:", totals.round(3).tolist())
print("mean with scaling:", round(totals.mean(), 3), " mean without scaling:", round(totals.mean() * (1 - p), 3), " spread:", round(totals.std(), 3))
test-time input: 0.77
inputs over the 8 masks: [0.0, 0.54, -0.6, -0.06, 1.6, 2.14, 1.0, 1.54]
mean with scaling: 0.77  mean without scaling: 0.385  spread: 0.896

Why dropout may help

A common explanation of why dropout helps is that a unit cannot rely on a particular partner being present, so it has to learn features that work with many different partners.

How many units are on?

With 100 hidden units and \(p = 0.5\), the number kept on a step is random with mean 50 and spread \(\sqrt{100\times0.5\times0.5} = 5\). Most steps keep between 40 and 60 units, so the sub-network has about the same size on all steps. The scaling by \(1/(1-p)\) fixes the mean, and the fluctuation stays as noise. A layer with 10 units keeps 5 on average with a spread of 1.6. Most steps keep between 2 and 8, so the size of the sub-network changes a lot.

In practice

Common values of \(p\) run from 0.1 to 0.5, and the largest are used on wide fully connected layers. Dropout usually helps most when the training set is small for the size of the network, as with a table of 600 records. It is often reduced or switched off when data is plentiful. It slows training because a step sees a noisier network, and it can interact badly with batch norm, since dropped units shift the variance that batch norm estimates. A common mistake is to leave the model in training mode at test time: the predictions are then random, and the same shark gets different answers on different runs.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If a model's test accuracy changes from run to run on fixed data, check model.eval() first. If training loss is much higher than expected and does not fall, try \(p = 0\): dropout may be too strong for a small network.

More questions

What does model.eval() change for a dropout layer and for a batch-norm layer?

Dropout stops dropping units and passes the values through unchanged, since the scaling by \(1/(1-p)\) was done in training. Batch norm stops using the batch and uses its stored averages. Forgetting it makes dropout predictions random and batch-norm predictions depend on the neighbours.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory Write the steps that give \(\mathrm{Var}(z) = n\sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}[x^2]\) for \(z = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i\). Then find the weight spread for a tanh layer with 256 inputs and for a ReLU layer with 256 inputs.

    Hint

    The terms \(w_i x_i\) are independent with mean 0, so variances add. It has \(\mathrm{Var}(w_i x_i) = \sigma^2\mathbb{E}[x_i^2]\). Then set the factor to 1 (tanh) or use the \(1/2\) for ReLU.

  2. theory A layer has 100 inputs and 50 outputs. Give the Xavier and He spreads and the limit \(a\) if the weights are drawn uniformly from \(-a\) to \(a\). Why must \(a\) be \(\sqrt{6/(n_{\text{in}}+n_{\text{out}})}\)?

    Hint

    Weights spread evenly over \(-a\) to \(a\) have variance \(a^2/3\).

  3. theory Normalise the row \((2, 4, 6, 8)\) with layer norm and with RMS norm (take \(\epsilon = 0\), \(\gamma = 1\), \(\beta = 0\)). Compare the means and the root mean squares of the two results.

  4. theory Show that \(\mathrm{Var}[\tilde a] = a^2 p/(1-p)\) for inverted dropout, and evaluate it for \(p = 0.2\) and \(a = 1\). For what \(p\) does the noise variance equal \(a^2\)?

Practice

  1. practice Build a 20-layer ReLU network in NumPy (width 100) and print the typical size at layers 1, 10 and 20 for the spreads 0.01, 0.1, 0.141 and 1. Check that the layer-20 sizes fall on the predictions of the factor \(n\sigma^2/2\) per layer.

  2. practice Write layer norm in five lines of NumPy and compare it with nn.LayerNorm on a random \(6\times 8\) batch (take care with eps and the variance definition). Then show that batch norm changes one shark's output when you change the other five sharks, and layer norm does not.

  3. practice Build the residual figure in NumPy: 30 tanh blocks of width 64 with weight scale 0.6, with and without \(x + F(x)\). Compare the slope reaching block 0 with the figure's numbers, and then add a layer norm after a block and see what happens to the activation size.

Think deeper

  1. open A 50-layer network with weight spread 0.01 does not learn with SGD. A friend says "use Adam, it rescales a weight's step, so the tiny slopes do not matter". Explain what Adam fixes and what it cannot fix here (B5).

  2. open SharkCam runs one frame at a time on a small computer. Which norm layers would you avoid, which would you keep, and what would you test before trusting the model on the robot (F2)?

  3. open You have only 100 labelled sharks and a network with 50,000 weights. Design an experiment on the made-up catch table that shows whether dropout helps, and say what you would measure and which values of \(p\) you would try.

Come back later

Try these after two days and again after a week, before you open the answers.

In B4, a chain of 30 ReLU layers with weight 0.8 gave a slope of 0.0015 at layer 1. Which fix in this chapter changes that factor, and which one adds a second path?

Choosing the spread (He) moves the weights toward a factor of 1 per layer. A residual connection adds a second path through the identity, so the factor per block is \(1 + f\) rather than \(f\).

Standardising the inputs (0.7, A2) and layer norm do the same thing to different numbers. What is the difference, and why does a hidden layer need its own?

Standardising rescales the input columns once, using the training set. A hidden layer's values change whenever the earlier weights change, so they have to be rescaled again at all steps, from numbers computed as the network runs.

Adam's \(v\) (B5) tracks the squared slope of a weight. If activations explode by a factor of \(10^{6}\), what happens to \(v\) for the weights of that layer, and to Adam's step?

The slope is large, so \(v\) is large, and the step \(\eta\,\hat m/\sqrt{\hat v}\) stays about \(\eta\). Adam is scale-free in the slope, so the step size does not explode. The exploded activations still break the forward pass, which Adam cannot repair.
